claims.claim: Camera distance and shot scale can be analyzed through such labels as long or establishing shot and close-up.
Introductory shot-scale vocabulary can include extreme close-up, close-up, medium close-up, medium shot, medium long shot, long shot, and extreme long shot.

A medium long shot is commonly described as framing a character from around the knees up and a medium shot from around the waist up, but these are practical reference points rather than universal measurements.
Shot scale can change what is visible in the frame and direct attention to a face, object, gesture, spatial relationship, or environment.
Shot scale differs from camera angle, camera movement, lens choice, and editing, even though a sequence can combine those choices.
Focal length affects angle of view and magnification, so onscreen scale does not by itself prove a specific lens or camera setup.
A defensible interpretation should describe visual evidence and sequence context rather than treat a shot size as a fixed emotional code or proof of intent.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Shot-size labels vary in exact boundaries across practices and sources.
positions: Common labels provide useful scale conventions.
The labels do not impose universal body-part measurements or fixed meanings.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses source-supported labels as flexible descriptive conventions and prioritizes precise visible evidence.
